30 of the 60
12 of the 60
items.explanation: Only a bill, a clinic letter, and a parcel slip mattered, about 5% of the pile.

items.prompt: What does curation mean in one line?
choices: Reading everything faster and more carefully
Deciding before reading what gets in at all
Saving every item to read later on
items.explanation: Curation is the earlier filter that decides what gets a look in the first place.

items.prompt: Why did Mara's hour not turn into knowledge?
choices: She did not spend enough time on it
She read the letters in the wrong order
Most of what she absorbed was noise
items.explanation: Volume she absorbed was mostly noise she then had to un-believe.

items.prompt: In a fast-moving field, how does volume compare with attention?
choices: Volume grows far past a fixed budget
Attention grows steadily to match all the new volume
The two stay about equal over time
items.explanation: Attention is a small fixed budget while volume is effectively unbounded.

items.prompt: What is hype?
choices: Any claim that appears in a newsletter
Loud, urgent-looking material, true or not
Information from sources you disagree with
items.explanation: Hype is defined by how it presents, not by whether it holds up.

items.prompt: Mara acted on 5 urgent-looking flyers. How many were empty?
choices: None of the 5
All 5 of them
4 of the 5
items.explanation: In the story four of the five urgent flyers turned out to be empty.

items.prompt: What is signal?
choices: Something real that is likely to hold up
Whatever arrives most often in a feed
Whatever the loudest voices repeat most often online
items.explanation: Signal has real substance behind it, however quietly it arrives.

items.prompt: Which fix does the unit point to for a pile you cannot finish?
choices: Check the pile more often each day
Filter harder before reading starts
Read faster to cover more material
items.explanation: The stream outgrows any reading pace, so the lever is filtering, not speed.

items.prompt: A neighbor tells Mara: 'just spend two hours instead of one and you will catch everything.' Why does this advice miss the problem?
choices: Two hours is still too little to open all 60 pieces
Longer reading makes the real letters easier to spot
She had opened all 60 already; sorting was the gap
Extra time only helps when spread across several days
items.explanation: Mara already looked at every piece in about an hour. What she lacked was a way to sort signal from hype, which more reading time does not provide.
items.reference:
Volume vs. attention (assumed mailbox numbers)
📬 60 pieces a week, 3 matter (5%)
🕐 Mara opens all 60: about 60 minutes
🚨 5 urgent-looking flyers, 4 empty
Why: attention is a small fixed budget, so the real question is what deserves to reach it at all.
items.learnMore:
Curation comes before reading

In a fast field, volume outgrows any attention budget. Reading faster does not close that gap, so the useful move is deciding, before reading, what gets in.

Common mistake

Treating a pile you cannot finish as a personal failing, when the pile is simply bigger than anyone's attention.
items.reflection: Think of an inbox, feed, or pile you feel behind on. How much of it genuinely mattered last week, and what would you have to decide before reading to keep only that?

items.prompt: Which statement about volume in a fast-moving field is correct?

It levels off once you follow enough sources, so effort pays off
It matters little, because most sources just repeat each other's claims
It shrinks over time as the field matures and its sources settle
items.explanation: Attention is fixed while volume keeps growing, so effort spent reading faster is aimed at the wrong lever.

A list of every flyer sent that week
A small tray of what looked like real mail
items.explanation: The tray is the filtered result: a few items that survived a quick check.

items.prompt: Why does Tomas trust the caretaker?

The caretaker has a friendly confident manner
The caretaker lives closest to the mailboxes
items.explanation: Trust rests on a track record, not on tone or convenience.

choices: Looks official, so pay it right away to avoid late fees
Looks official, unconfirmed, so check before paying
Looks fake, so throw it out unopened

items.prompt: What is batching?
choices: Checking every source every few minutes
Saving everything for one yearly big review
Looking at what is new on a fixed schedule
items.explanation: Batching means a fixed, repeating review time, such as once a week.

items.prompt: What does a trusted curator do?
choices: Reads the flood for you and passes on what held up
Writes extra new posts for you to read each day
Reads only the items that you personally send them
items.explanation: The curator absorbs the volume so you review only the survivors.

items.prompt: About how long did Tomas spend on his mail per week?
choices: About 60 minutes
About 6 minutes
About 6 hours
items.explanation: A tray of 4 items took roughly 6 minutes in the story.

items.prompt: When choosing a filter, what matters most?
choices: Whether it posts the most often each day
Whether it sounds the most certain
Whether its past picks actually held up
items.explanation: Confidence and volume are cheap to fake; a record is not.

items.prompt: How many of the 60 pieces did the caretaker drop?
choices: 56 of them
4 of them
30 of them
items.explanation: Of 60 pieces, 4 were passed on, so 56 never reached Tomas.

items.prompt: A neighbor says to Tomas: 'you only see what the caretaker chose, so you miss things.' Which reply is strongest?
choices: Fair, so he should open all 60 pieces himself every week just to be safe
The 56 dropped were nearly all noise, and the 3 real ones still arrived
The caretaker's choices can never be wrong, so nothing is ever missed
Fair, but nothing in the mail really matters, so a miss costs nothing
items.explanation: A filter can drop things; the question is what it drops. Here the 56 were noise, the 3 real letters came through, and doubt was labeled.
items.reference:
Tomas's tray (assumed numbers)
📥 60 pieces in, 56 dropped, 4 passed on
🕐 about 6 minutes a week
🏷️ one item flagged: check before paying
Why: a filter with a record reads the flood for you and says honestly what it could not confirm.
items.learnMore:
What makes a filter trustworthy

A trusted curator is someone whose past picks held up. Their value is the reading they do on your behalf plus honest labels on what is unresolved, not authority by tone.

Common mistake

Choosing a filter because it sounds sure or posts often, when only a record of being right is hard to fake.
items.reflection: Who already acts as a filter for you in some area of life? What evidence do you actually have that their picks hold up?

items.prompt: Caretaker A has sorted this building's mail for years and flags uncertain items. Caretaker B is new, fast-talking, and very sure. Whose tray should Tomas rely on?

A, because a record of good sorting is costly to fake
A, because older people never make sorting errors
items.explanation: Confidence is free to produce, while a record of held-up calls is not. A's flags of doubt add further honest information.

items.prompt: In the model, about how many useful items does the field produce per week?
choices: About 20 items
About 2 items
About 200 items
items.explanation: The model assumes a small roughly fixed amount of useful signal, about 2 a week.

items.prompt: What shape does the useful-items curve have as hours rise?
choices: Rises in a straight line forever
Stays flat, then jumps up late
Rises fast, then flattens
items.explanation: Early hours take the easy finds, so gains taper hard.

items.prompt: About how much does the first hour surface?
choices: About 0.52 items
About 1.9 items
About 0.05 items
items.explanation: At 1 hour the model gives roughly 0.52 of the 2 items.

items.prompt: What would hours 11 to 15 add in the model?
choices: About 1 more item
About 0.08 items
About 2 more items
items.explanation: Going from 10 to 15 hours moves the curve from 1.90 to 1.98.

items.prompt: Which hours buy the most new signal?
choices: The last few hours
All hours about equally
The first few hours
items.explanation: The curve is steepest at the start.

items.prompt: At 10 hours, roughly what share of the useful items does the model say Elena surfaces?
choices: About 95%
About 50%
About 10%
items.explanation: 1.90 of 2 is about 95%, but at ten times the time of the first hour.

items.prompt: After the curve flattens, what do extra raw hours mostly add?
choices: A steady flow of newly found signal
Mostly noise, very little signal
Faster learning of every claim
items.explanation: The useful items are mostly already found; more reading brings more of the rest.

items.prompt: Once the curve is flat, which lever is better?
choices: Reading for more hours
Checking more often in the day
Filtering before reading
items.explanation: More hours is the lever that has run out; filtering changes what reaches you.

items.prompt: In the model, a reader raises raw reading from 5 to 10 hours a week. What does the extra time buy?
choices: About 1.55 more useful items
About 0.9 more useful items
About 2 more useful items
About 0.35 more useful items
items.explanation: At 5 hours the curve is near 1.55 and at 10 hours near 1.90, so five more hours add about 0.35.
items.reference:
Modeled useful items per week (assumed, ceiling 2)
1 hr: 0.52 | 3 hrs: 1.19
5 hrs: 1.55 | 10 hrs: 1.90
15 hrs: 1.98 (hours 11 to 15 add 0.08)
Why: each extra raw-reading hour finds a smaller share of what is left, so the curve flattens.
items.learnMore:
Why the curve flattens

If the field only yields about 2 useful items a week, each hour can only find some share of what remains. The first hours take the easy finds; later hours mostly re-read noise.

Common mistake

Reading the flat part of the curve as a reason to read even more, when it is the sign that reading is the wrong lever.
items.reflection: Pick a habit where you keep adding hours. Where on its curve are you now, and what did the first hour buy compared with the tenth?

items.explanation: 0.52 divided by 1.90 is about 27%. One tenth of the time already gets roughly a quarter of the signal.

items.prompt: What are the two jobs of the funnel?
choices: Shrink the volume and add a delay
Add volume and remove the delay
Speed up posts and amplify them
items.explanation: Fewer items reach you, and they arrive after some scrutiny.

items.prompt: In the funnel, what happens to most items?
choices: They reach you with a warning label
They are dropped and never reach you
They are saved in a long unread backlog
items.explanation: Most of the stream is dropped upstream.

items.prompt: Why does the delay help?
choices: Older claims are always more correct than new ones
Readers get time to write long replies online
Claims face some scrutiny before repeating
items.explanation: A fizzle cannot be told from a real finding on day one, so time helps sort them.

items.prompt: Which step comes last in the funnel?
choices: Batched review on a fixed schedule
The raw stream of everything published
A new round of raw checking each day
items.explanation: Raw stream, then filters, then a scheduled review of the survivors.

items.prompt: Does Diego see the same 5 claims as Elena, just later?
choices: Yes, only the timing differs between the two of them
No, he sees a smaller set that survived a week
Yes, but with extra hype added later
items.explanation: The filter drops most claims, so what he sees is different, not just late.

items.prompt: Which two parts of the funnel did Elena skip?
choices: Batching and the weekly review
Reading it all and acting on it
Volume reduction and the delay
items.explanation: She read the raw stream directly, so nothing reduced or delayed it.

items.prompt: Why can't a curator drop a fizzle the moment it is published?
choices: A fizzle cannot yet be told from a real finding
Curators only ever work on weekends and holidays
Fizzles are always the most popular items
items.explanation: That is exactly why the delay exists.

items.prompt: How often does Diego review his digest?
choices: Every hour, in short bursts
Once a week, in one sitting
Once a year, in one sitting
items.explanation: Batching means one scheduled review, here weekly.

items.prompt: Which description of the funnel's middle step is accurate?
choices: It drops most items, so a different, smaller set reaches you
It relays everything to you, only after a short delay in each case
It re-orders items so that the loudest ones always arrive first
It adds commentary but changes nothing about what arrives
items.explanation: Dropping, not relaying, is what makes the set that arrives different from the raw stream.
items.reference:
The funnel
🌊 raw stream: everything published
🧰 trusted filters: most items dropped
🗓️ batched review: once, on a schedule
Why: the funnel shrinks volume and adds a delay, and the drop is what changes what reaches you.
items.learnMore:
Drop, not just delay

The delay lets a claim face scrutiny, which makes dropping possible. But the value is in the drop: you see a different, smaller set, not the same set later.

Common mistake

Thinking a curator only relays the stream on a lag, when the point is that most of it never gets repeated.
items.reflection: Describe a place where something stands between a flood and you. What does it drop, and how would you notice if it started dropping the wrong things?

items.prompt: A curator repeats a claim the day it appears with no check. What has the funnel lost for that claim?

The reduction that removes duplicate coverage of one story
The track record that lets you weight the source's calls
The delay that lets it face scrutiny before reaching you
items.explanation: Passing a claim on at once removes the time in which fizzles get walked back. Volume reduction and track record are separate parts.

Both act on the same count, as both see the claims
Y acts on more, since a curator adds extra weight
items.explanation: Time before belief is the point: claims that fizzle in the first week never reach Y.

items.prompt: What does the recency check say?
choices: New always beats older claims made before it
Old claims are always stale
New is not automatically important
items.explanation: Newness alone is not significance.

items.prompt: What does regression to the mean say about early claims?
choices: The loudest ones tend to be overstated
Quiet claims are always false in these fields
Early claims are always understated
items.explanation: Extreme early versions tend to moderate with more evidence.

items.prompt: What does track-record trust say?
choices: Weight a source by how confident it sounds
Weight a source by whether its past calls held up
Weight a source by how often it posts
items.explanation: A source's record, not its tone, sets its weight.

items.prompt: Which of these is expensive to fake?
choices: A confident, fluent tone
A dramatic, attention-grabbing headline
A record of being right before
items.explanation: Tone and headlines are free; a held-up record is not.

items.prompt: A brand-new, dramatic claim comes from a source with no record. What is the odds-based move?
choices: Down-weight it and watch for a week
Dismiss it forever as plain hype from the start
Act on it today to be early
items.explanation: Heuristics buy time before belief, not a permanent verdict.

items.prompt: Do the heuristics guarantee catching every fizzle?
choices: Yes, if all three are applied
No, they only shift the odds
Yes, if applied to the loudest items
items.explanation: They are heuristics, not proof.

items.prompt: Which claim looks most like hype?
choices: Old, modest, and repeated by three studies
Slow-moving and dull from a proven source
New, dramatic, unreplicated, from no known record
items.explanation: That combination is the profile of Elena's four fizzles.

items.prompt: What does regression to the mean predict about an extreme early claim?
choices: It will probably moderate with more evidence
It will probably grow with more evidence
It will probably vanish without any further trace
items.explanation: The extreme version is the one most likely to be pulled back toward reality.

items.prompt: Source A is new this week, with a 'changes everything' headline and no record. Source B has five years of calls that held up and says 'promising, not confirmed.' Which gets more weight, and why?
choices: A, because a bolder claim carries more information
A, because newer sources have fewer old biases
B, because a record of held-up calls is costly to fake
B, because calm wording proves the claim is true
items.explanation: Weight follows record, not boldness. Calm wording is not itself proof; the record is what is hard to fake.
items.reference:
Three heuristics
🆕 Recency: new is not automatically important
📉 Regression: loud early claims tend to moderate
🏅 Track record: weight past calls that held up
Why: they shift the odds on a claim before proof exists; they are not a verdict.
items.learnMore:
Odds, not verdicts

A brand-new, dramatic claim from a source with no record is likely overstated, but not certainly. Down-weight it, let it sit, and see whether it survives.

Common mistake

Dismissing every newcomer's claim forever, or acting on it at once because it is exciting.

A newcomer has no record to weight, so the first job is observing whose calls hold up. A veteran of a high-stakes field also has to set the interval against what lateness costs.
